title: Sagas & Distributed Transactions
subtitle: Watch one order touch three services, see why a global lock breaks, and see how a saga undoes work instead.
learn: Why two-phase commit (2PC) blocks and why most microservice teams avoid it
How a saga replaces one big transaction with a chain of small local ones
The difference between orchestration and choreography, and when each fits
How compensating actions undo earlier steps, and why they must be idempotent and retried
What a saga cannot give you: isolation between concurrent sagas

steps.title: One order, three databases
steps.body: A customer places an order. That means charging a card (Payment DB), reserving stock (Inventory DB), and booking a courier (Shipping DB). Each service owns its own database, so no single BEGIN ... COMMIT covers all three. What happens if the card is charged but the courier booking fails? This lesson is about keeping those three writes consistent without one shared transaction.
steps.idea: Once data is split across services, a single ACID transaction (atomic, consistent, isolated, durable) no longer spans the whole business operation.
steps.caption: Three services, each owning its data.

steps.title: The classic answer: two-phase commit
steps.body: Two-phase commit adds a coordinator. In phase one it asks every participant to PREPARE: do the work, take locks, and promise you can commit. In phase two, if all said yes, it tells everyone to COMMIT; otherwise ABORT. With 5 ms round trips this takes roughly 10 to 20 ms, and the rows stay locked the whole time. Here the Order service plays coordinator.
steps.idea: 2PC gives all-or-nothing atomicity by making every participant hold locks until the coordinator decides.
steps.caption: Votes collected, then COMMIT sent; locks held throughout.

steps.title: Why 2PC hurts at scale
steps.body: Suppose the coordinator crashes after collecting the YES votes but before sending its decision. Every participant is stuck: it promised to commit, so it cannot abort alone. It keeps its locks until the coordinator recovers; an operator can force a heuristic decision, but that risks inconsistency. Assume the restart takes 30 seconds, and orders on those rows queue behind the locks. Even with no crash, one slow or down participant stalls everyone. Across independent services and third-party APIs (a card processor does not speak XA, the standard 2PC protocol for databases) 2PC is rarely an option.
steps.idea: 2PC blocks on coordinator failure, and it is a poor fit across independently owned services and third-party APIs.
steps.caption: Coordinator died; three services hold locks.

steps.title: The saga idea
steps.body: A saga drops the global lock. It splits the business operation into a sequence of local transactions, one per service. Each commits immediately and releases its locks. If a later step fails, the saga runs a compensating action for every step already done, such as refunding a payment. The data is briefly inconsistent while the saga runs (eventual consistency: all services agree once the saga finishes), and that is the price: you trade atomicity and isolation for availability. Assume each step takes about 10 ms including a 5 ms round trip, and each local lock lasts about 3 ms.
steps.idea: A saga is a series of local commits plus a planned undo for each, giving eventual consistency instead of atomicity.
steps.caption: Each step commits alone and frees its locks.

steps.title: Orchestration: a conductor drives it
steps.body: Here is the flow up to the last step. In an orchestrated saga one component, here the Order service, holds the workflow. Payment was already charged in the previous step; the orchestrator now commands Inventory, then Shipping, waiting for each reply. The order of steps and the failure rules live in one place, often a persisted state machine, so it can resume after a crash. Each service just does its local job and answers.
steps.idea: Orchestration puts the saga's flow in one place that tells each service what to do next.
steps.caption: Orchestrator commands each step in turn.

steps.title: A step fails: run the undo steps
steps.body: Shipping finds no courier is available and replies with a failure. Its own transaction rolled back, so there is nothing to undo there. The orchestrator walks backwards: release the reserved stock, then refund the charge. A compensation is a new forward action, not a database rollback, because earlier steps already committed. Order steps so ones likely to fail come early and hard-to-undo ones come late, after the pivot. Card processors let you authorize first and capture only at the pivot (the go/no-go step), so an early failure is a cheap void, not a visible refund. After the pivot commits you retry forward. If a reply times out, treat the outcome as unknown and compensate anyway.
steps.idea: Compensating actions are new transactions that semantically reverse committed steps, run in reverse order.
steps.caption: Failure triggers refund and stock release.

steps.title: Choreography: services react to events
steps.body: The alternative has no conductor. The Order service publishes OrderPlaced on the event bus. Payment reacts and publishes PaymentTaken, Inventory reacts and publishes StockReserved, and Shipping reacts to that. Every service knows only which events it listens to and emits. There is no central coordinator to fail, though the event bus itself must be highly available. Adding a listener needs no change to the others, but nobody holds the whole flow. Each bus hop adds about 5 ms of publish and deliver time, so this run takes about 30 ms.
steps.idea: Choreography encodes the saga as a chain of events, with no central coordinator and no single place that shows the whole flow.
steps.caption: Events pass the baton through the bus.

steps.title: Choosing between the two
steps.body: As a rule of thumb, choreography suits short sagas of two to four steps with few owners, because it is simple and loosely coupled. Past that, the event chain becomes hard to follow and cyclic dependencies creep in, so orchestration pays off: one place to read, test, time out, and monitor the flow. Orchestrators add a component to run and can attract business logic, so keep them to sequencing only. In choreography a failure is just another event: Shipping emits ShipFailed, Inventory releases stock, and Payment reacts to that to refund. (Payment could also listen to ShipFailed directly.)
steps.idea: Choreography wins on coupling for small flows; orchestration wins on visibility once flows grow or branch.
steps.caption: Choreographed failure: ShipFailed -> stock released -> refund.

steps.title: Retries, duplicates, and dirty reads
steps.body: Messages are usually delivered at least once, so every step and compensation must be idempotent: refunding twice must not refund twice, so key each command with the saga and step ID. Retry compensations with backoff, and alert a human if one cannot succeed. Write the local change and the outgoing message in one local transaction (a transactional outbox) so a crash cannot lose the next step. Since each step is visible once committed, another request can see an item as reserved early; semantic locks, such as a PENDING flag, help.
steps.idea: Sagas need idempotent steps and explicit handling of intermediate state, because they offer no isolation.
steps.caption: Duplicate refund command is ignored.

steps.title: Atomic, or available
steps.body: 2PC gives atomic commits across services but blocks on coordinator failure and holds locks, so it is rare between microservices. A saga gives up atomicity and isolation: each local transaction commits, and failures trigger compensations in reverse order. Pick orchestration for longer or branching flows and choreography for short ones. Make every step idempotent and plan for intermediate states.
steps.idea: Replace one big lock with small commits and planned undo steps, and design for the in-between.
steps.caption: Local commits plus compensations.

quiz.q: A 2PC coordinator crashes after all participants voted YES but before it sent COMMIT. What is the main problem?
options: Participants abort immediately and the order is lost
Participants keep their locks and wait for a decision
Participants commit by themselves after a short timeout
The vote results are replayed from the event bus
quiz.why: Having voted YES, a participant promised it can commit and cannot safely abort or commit without the decision, so it blocks while holding locks.

quiz.q: In a saga, the payment step has committed and shipping then reports that no courier is available. What is the correct recovery?
options: Roll back the payment database transaction
Retry shipping forever and leave payment as is
Run a compensating action such as a refund
Delete the payment row directly from the Payment DB
quiz.why: The payment transaction already committed and released its locks, so it cannot be rolled back. A new forward action, the refund, reverses its business effect.

quiz.q: Your saga has seven steps with conditional branches and the team keeps losing track of where an order is stuck. Which change helps most?
options: Switch to choreography so each service owns less
Use 2PC for the last three steps of the flow
Remove every compensation to simplify the flow
Orchestrate it with a stored workflow state
quiz.why: Orchestration puts the flow and its current state in one place, which makes long or branching sagas readable, testable, and monitorable.

quiz.q: A refund command is delivered twice because of a retry. Why is that safe in a well-built saga?
options: The event bus guarantees exactly-once delivery everywhere
The refund is idempotent, keyed by saga and step ID
Sagas hold a global lock during compensation
Retries are disabled during compensation
quiz.why: At-least-once delivery means duplicates happen, so each step and compensation must detect a repeat via an idempotency key and do nothing the second time.

quiz.q: While one order's saga is mid-flight, a second request reads the last item as reserved, but that saga may still fail and release it. Which tool reduces this problem?
options: Hold row locks in all three databases until the saga ends
Retry compensations faster
A bigger event bus
Mark the item PENDING (a semantic lock) so others know it is mid-saga
quiz.why: Sagas commit each step early and give no isolation, so other requests can see half-finished state. A semantic lock such as a PENDING flag tells them the reservation may still be undone, so they can wait, warn, or treat it as uncertain. Holding cross-database locks for the whole saga is exactly the blocking that sagas avoid.

cheatsheet.def: Coordinator asks all participants to PREPARE, then COMMIT or ABORT. Atomic, but blocking and lock-heavy.
A sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action, giving eventual consistency across services.
A central orchestrator sends commands to each step and owns the flow and failure rules. Better for long flows.
Services react to each other's events with no central coordinator. Loosely coupled, but the flow is implicit.
A new transaction that semantically undoes a committed step, such as a refund. Run in reverse order and retried until it succeeds.
An ID sent with each command so a duplicate delivery is recognised and ignored.
A status flag like PENDING that marks data as mid-saga so other requests treat it carefully.
The go/no-go step of a saga. Steps before it are compensatable; once it commits, the saga is committed to finishing, and later steps are retried until they succeed.
